extracted.intended_audience: general readers and critics of poetry (including inexperienced readers of Lyrical Ballads)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for readers on how to judge and appreciate poetry, emphasising content, genuine feeling, openness to new forms, and the development of taste. Aimed at guiding personal critical responses rather than technical metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter (content) is primary
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not from the metre, not from the language, not from the order of the words; but the matter expressed in Dr. Johnson's stanza is contemptible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem first by what it says (its matter/content) rather than by metre, diction, or word-order alone. Trivial or simple verses should be treated as wanting sense if they are neither interesting in themselves nor capable of leading to anything interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the poem interest and lead to thought or feeling?
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is neither interesting in itself, nor can lead to any thing interesting; the images neither originate in that sane state of feeling which arises out of thought, nor can excite thought or feeling in the Reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the poem provokes thought or genuine feeling. A successful poem's images should arise from a sane state of feeling grounded in thought and should be capable of exciting similar thought or feeling in the reader; lack of this is a sign of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide genus before species (establish basic quality first)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why trouble yourself about the species till you have previously decided upon the genus? Why take pains to prove that an Ape is not a Newton when it is self-evident that he is not a man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the poem's fundamental status (e.g., whether it is genuinely poetic or substantively good) before arguing fine distinctions or classifications of style/genre. Don't waste effort on taxonomy if the foundational quality is absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by your own genuine feelings, not social conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have one request to make of my Reader, which is, that in judging these Poems he would decide by his own feelings genuinely, and not by reflection upon what will probably be the judgment of others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allowing imagined opinions of others to shape your judgment. Critics often excuse their own tastes by appealing to what 'certain classes' will think; this undermines sound, unadulterated judgment. Respond authentically to your own feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give an author the presumption of ability from a good composition
rubrics_metrics.description: "If an Author by any single composition has impressed us with respect for his talents, it is useful to consider this as affording a presumption, that, on other occasions where we have been displeased, he nevertheless may not have written ill or absurdly; and, further, to give him so much credit for this one composition as may induce us to review what has displeased us with more care..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an author has produced a work that commands respect, allow that accomplishment to temper your judgment of their other, less satisfactory pieces. Revisit works that initially displeased you with more care rather than dismissing the author out of hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate taste by study; temper rash decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: "An accurate taste in Poetry and in all the other arts... is an acquired talent, which can only be produced by thought and a long continued intercourse with the best models of composition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that sound critical taste is developed over time by thoughtful exposure to exemplary works. Inexperienced readers should still judge, but they should temper rashness and accept the possibility of error in their immediate judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be open to new poetic pleasures even if it requires giving up old preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Reader is himself conscious of the pleasure which he has received from such composition... we not only wish to be pleased, but to be pleased in that particular way in which we have been accustomed to be pleased... in order entirely to enjoy the Poetry which I am recommending, it would be necessary to give up much of what is ordinarily enjoyed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise personal attachment to familiar poetic forms and be willing to relinquish some habitual pleasures in order to appreciate new or different kinds of poetry. Openness can reveal purer, more lasting, or more exquisite enjoyments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess for permanence and moral significance
rubrics_metrics.description: "a species of poetry would be produced, which is genuine poetry; in its nature well adapted to interest mankind permanently, and likewise important in the multiplicity and quality of its moral relations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a poem possesses qualities that will give it lasting interest and whether it bears on moral or ethical dimensions of human experience. Genuine poetry, insofar as it is valuable, should be able to engage permanently and relate richly to moral life.
